and there was no worry of interruption or disturbance. There was
nothing in my work to call for any special ability; it was merely
copying. All that I had to do was to sit and copy.


"Well, I thought over the matter all day, and began to think
that I might have done better. After all, 4 pounds a week was
not very much, when everything was taken into consideration. My
business was poor, and I had to work hard to make ends meet. However,
I was pleased at the idea that I should be doing something, even
if it were only copying out the Encyclopaedia Britannica, and then
when I looked at the advertisement again I thought it was quite
a remarkable position, and that the money was not to be despised
either. It would at least help keep my head above water."

"Did you not see anything peculiar about the office?" asked
Holmes.

"Well, I thought that my good fortune was to begin next day, but
I was very much mistaken. I was punctual to the minute, and found
Mr. Duncan Ross there before me. He welcomed me kindly, and showed
me my chair and my desk, which was just a plain wooden one, with
nothing upon it save a few pens, ink, and blotting-paper. I sat
down and started to work. I copied from the first page of the A’s
and so I went on copying all day, and next day and next day, and
so on, until nearly two months had gone over.

"Well, I thought at first that it was a bit of a lark, and that
my assistant, Vincent Spaulding, was pulling my leg; but when I
got to the office next morning and found everything as he had
described it, I began to think that he was right. There was the
table all ready, and a chair, and the inkstand, and a brand-new
pen. I sat down and commenced copying.

"It was not very interesting work. The Encyclopaedia is a very
tedious work, and there is no chance for imagination. Still, it
was better than doing nothing, and the money was very welcome. It
was not quite so pleasant, however, as the other work which I had
to do, for my business was beginning to prosper, and I did not
wish to neglect it; and then, again, the copying was so very
tedious."

"Well, I started next morning, punctual to the minute, at ten
o'clock. There was no one in the office except the copying-clerk,
who was a freckled, snub-nosed boy. I found my place at the table,
and to my surprise and delight, got so interested in my work
that the time slipped away very quickly. The boy brought me my
lunch, and I copied until two. Then, with a few farewell words
to the boy, I left the building and did not return again for some
weeks."

"You did not think it worth while to continue copying the
'Encyclopaedia Britannica'?"

"Not exactly," said the pawnbroker. "I quite overlooked it, Mr.
Holmes. The fact is, that I soon found out that there was nothing
else to copy. The business was to copy for four hours a day, but
after I had done this for a week, I found that only a few pages
had been copied. The book had been opened, but never again
touched."

"What did you do?"

"Well, I thought over the matter all day, and by evening I was in
low spirits again; for I had quite persuaded myself that the
whole affair must be some great hoax or fraud, though what its
object might be I could not imagine. It seemed altogether past
belief that anyone could make such a will, or that they would pay
such a sum for doing anything so simple as copying out the
'Encyclopaedia Britannica.' Vincent Spaulding did what he could to
cheer me up, but by bedtime I had reasoned myself out of the
whole thing. However, in the morning I determined to have a look
at it anyhow, so I bought a penny bottle of ink, and with a
quill-pen, and seven sheets of foolscap paper, I started off for
Pope's Court.

"Eight weeks passed in this way, Mr. Holmes, and I had written
about Abbots and Archery and Armadillos, when my luck came to an
end. To begin at the beginning. It was on a Tuesday that it
happened. I went to my work as usual at ten o'clock, but I found
the door shut and locked. I tried the door, of course, and then
I looked through the window, but no one was there, and the place
was empty. I was naturally very angry, as you can imagine, and I
was going to burst the door open when I heard steps behind me and
turning round I saw Mr. Duncan Ross.

"Eight weeks passed away like this, and I had written about
half of the A's of the Encyclopaedia, when I began to feel that
things were not quite as they should be. It seemed odd that my
employer should never come to look me over. I tried to get a
glance into his private room, but the door was always locked, and
there was no window to it. I have also noticed that the
building was empty except for my office and his own.

"Eight weeks passed in this way, Mr. Holmes, and I had written
about Abbotsford and then nearly all of Abercrombie when one
morning I came in and found that my chair was gone. I was not
only surprised, but considerably put out, for I had not been able
to finish my work as I was anxious to do. My assistant, Mr.
Spaulding, he came to me at once with a very worried look upon
his face, and he asks me if I had heard what had happened to the
League.

"No, said I, what is it, then?

"Why, said he, the League is broken up!"


"Eight weeks passed away like this, and I had written about
Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture and Attica, and
I was beginning to think all was right, when I woke up one
morning, Mr. Holmes, and found that something had happened. I
don't know whether I have made myself quite clear."

"Not quite," said Holmes. "Perhaps you would do well to resume
your account from the point where you found that something had
happened. What was that something?"

"Eight weeks passed in this way, Mr. Holmes, and I had written and
rewritten the whole of the A's of the 'Encyclopaedia Britannica'
twice over before it occurred to me to ask myself why I was doing
it. It was so preposterous that I felt my hair would turn white
if I thought of it any longer. It was so stupid that I felt an
impulse to give the whole thing up there and then. And then it
came over me that there must be something more to it than that."

"Eight weeks passed away like this, and I had written about
Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture and Attica, and
hoped with diligence that I might get on to the B's before very
long. It cost me something in foolscap, and I had pretty nearly
filled a shelf with my writings. And then suddenly the whole
business came to an end."

"To an end?"

"No, no," cried Holmes, shoving his chair back and his long legs
stretching out in front of him.  "I beg your pardon. I assure you
that it is most interesting.  I particularly want to hear all
about it, and especially what you did upon receiving this
announcement."

"My dear Mr. Wilson," said Holmes, his laughter bubbling over
again, "pray do not be offended. But the facts are so
extraordinary, the situation so whimsical, that we must really
excuse ourselves for giving way to our mirth.  The thing is so
utterly preposterous that the only possible way of treating it is
to laugh at it."

"I don't understand it at all," said Jabez Wilson. "I am sure that
I have never done anything to make anyone treat me in such a way
as that."

"No, no," cried Holmes, checking his laughter and rising from his
chair.  "I beg your pardon.  It is just that the incident is so
singular.  But you are quite right to be annoyed.  Let us look at
the matter seriously.  You say that within the last few days you
have not seen Mr. Duncan Ross?"
"No, no, my dear sir, I assure you that it is not with the intention of
laughing at you that we give way to this mirth," said Holmes,
controlling his laughter with difficulty. "The matter is really
one of some amusement."

"I cannot see it," insisted Mr. Jabez Wilson. "There is nothing to
laugh about in the matter."

"On the contrary, my dear sir, it is exceedingly amusing. You
must not be angry with us. It is a most singular and, I must
confess, ludicrous case. But we must have the details before we
can venture to make any explanation."

"No, no," cried Holmes, shoving his chair back and leaning
forward, his eyes twinkling.  "I beg your pardon. I assure you
that I was never more serious in my life. But you are too quick,
Mr. Wilson. You have not told us the best part of the story yet.
It is certainly a most singular business, and one which would
puzzle the best criminalist in Europe. The question is, what
was the object of this rather fantastic business?"

"No, no," cried Holmes, shoving him back into the chair from
which he had half risen. "I really wouldn't miss your case for
the world. It is most refreshingly unusual. But there is, if you
will excuse my saying so, something just a little funny about it.
Pray what steps did you take when you found the card upon the
door?"

"And you did very wisely," said Holmes. "Your case is an
extraordinary one, and I think that it is possible that we may
find a solution. Now let me have the facts again, briefly,
without any of those embellishments which only serve to make the
matter more complicated. What was the advertisement that started
the whole affair?"  Holmes leaned back and closed his eyes,
tapping his long, thin fingers together.  "Just state the facts as
you did to me at the beginning, Mr. Wilson.  Let us begin again
from the very start."
"And you did very wisely," said Holmes.  "Now, let us consider
the facts.  You say that this Mr. Duncan Ross, or William Morris,
or whatever his name is, was a solicitor.  What sort of person
was he?"
"And you did very wisely," said Holmes. "Now, let us consider the
facts. You say that within the last three months you have
gradually become aware that Mr. Spaulding has not been spending
all his evenings at his lodgings. Is that so?"

"Yes, sir. He used to go out very early and come home very late.
And very often he was away for days."


"And you did very wisely," said Holmes. "Your case is an
interesting one, and I shall make a point of looking into it.
You did not, of course, go to the place yourself where you were
employed?"

"No, sir. It was too far away from my home."

"And you don't know what the League was doing with you?"

"No, sir. But I should like to know."

"I don't think that I can help you much," said Holmes, smiling,
"without looking into the matter. But what is this assistant of
yours like? Is he a respectable fellow?"

"Yes, sir. One could not wish for a better. It is very curious,
but I have never been able to find out anything about him."

"Indeed? That is the most curious part of it all. Well, I shall
have to see the place, I fancy. And I think that I will have to
see your assistant, too."

"And you did very wisely," said Holmes. "Now, let us consider
the facts. We have the advertisement, the four pounds a week, the
copying of the Encyclopaedia, the sudden cessation of the
employment, and, finally, the curious disappearance of the
employer. That is quite enough to work upon."

"And I have the address," I added. "I have that address in my
pocket. It is 7 Pope's Court, Fleet Street."

"Very good," said Holmes. "Now, let us go there. I am sure that
we shall find something worth seeing."

"And you did very wisely," said Holmes. "Your case is an
exceedingly remarkable one, and I shall be happy to look into it.
From what you have told me I think that it is possible that
graver issues hang from it than might at first sight appear."

"Grave enough!" said Mr. Jabez Wilson. "Why, I have lost four
pound a week."

"Precisely. Now let us consider the facts. You received a
circular from some unknown body, which offered you this
extraordinary employment at four pounds a week for a purely
nominal service. At the address given you found a man who
appeared to be the manager of the institution."

"Precisely," said Holmes.  "And now let us proceed to business.
You are quite sure that this Spaulding is a respectable young man?"
"We shall endeavor to clear up these points for you. You have
mentioned that your assistant, Mr. Spaulding, proposed your
application for this sinecure?"

"Yes, sir. He was the one who saw the advertisement."

"Precisely," said Holmes. "Now, let us consider the matter a
little more closely. You say that, apart from this curious
business of the Red-headed League, you have nothing to complain
of in connection with your assistant, Mr. Spaulding?"

"Precisely," said Holmes.  "Now let us consider the facts.  You
were employed to copy the Encyclopaedia Britannica.  The work was
purely nominal, and yet it was imperative that you should remain
in the office during business hours, and that you should not leave
the building.  Had you done so, your employment would have
ceased.  These facts are all important to us."
"We shall endeavour to clear up these points for you. And, first,
one or two questions, Mr. Wilson. This assistant of yours who
first called your attention to the advertisement--how long had he
been with you?"

"About a month then."

"How did he come?"

"In answer to an advertisement."

"Was he the only applicant?"

"No, I had a dozen."

"Why did you pick him?"

"Because he was handy and would come cheap."

"At half-wages, in fact."

"Yes."

"What is he like, this Vincent Spaulding?"

"Small, stout-built, very quick in his ways, no hair on his face,
though he's not short of thirty. Has a white splash of acid upon
his forehead."

Holmes sat up in his chair in considerable excitement. "I thought
as much," said he. "Have you ever observed that his ears are
pierced for earrings?"

"Yes, sir. He told me that a gipsy had done it for him when he
was a lad."

"Hum!" said Holmes, sinking back in deep thought. "He is still
with you?"

"Oh, yes, sir; I have only just left him."

"And has your business been attended to in your absence?"

"Nothing to complain of, sir. There's never very much to do of a
morning."

"That will do, Mr. Wilson. I shall be happy to give you an
opinion upon the subject in the course of a day or two. To-day is
Saturday, and I hope that by Monday we may come to a conclusion."

"Well, Watson," said Holmes when our visitor had left us, "what
do you make of it all?"

"I make nothing of it," I answered frankly. "It is a most
mysterious business."

"To Saxe-Coburg Square, I think, Watson. It is quite on the cards
that we may find something which may help us. In any case,
nothing could be more instructive than a personal visit to the
scene of action. Come along, then."

"To Saxe-Coburg Square, I think, first of all. It is just
possible that we might find something which would interest us
there."  He took his hat and his stick, and set off at once for
the address of our client.  I accompanied him, of course.

"To call upon Mr. Vincent Spaulding, of course. He is a
character who is worth investigation. I shall see him this
afternoon, and I think that I may very likely learn more from him
than from all the printed matter in London. Meanwhile, you may
make up your mind that this is quite one of the most singular
cases which we have ever handled."

"To Saxe-Coburg Square, I think, Watson. It is a bijou
pawnbroker's business, but it may prove a very important one to
us. I propose to call upon this young Spaulding, and to spend
some hours in his company. I shall see whether he really has
been in China. You may accompany me if you wish."

"To call upon Mr. Vincent Spaulding, of course," he answered,
"and to spend some hours in his delightful company. I wish you
would come with me, Watson."

"I should be very happy," I replied.

"Not now, my dear fellow. Later in the day. There are one or two
things which I would wish to do first. I am going out now to
consult Professor Moriarty, the famous criminal expert, upon one
or two points which have puzzled me. Then I have several things
to attend to before we can proceed to Saxe-Coburg Square."

"Professor Moriarty?" I asked, with some surprise. "But I thought
he had gone abroad."

"His whereabouts is known to me," said Holmes, with a significant
smile. "A most interesting and charming man, though, like all
genius, somewhat eccentric in his notions."
"To smoke," he answered. "It is quite a three pipe problem, and I
beg that you won't speak to me for fifty minutes." He curled
himself up in his chair, with his thin knees drawn up to his
hawk-like nose, and there he sat with his eyes closed and his
black clay pipe thrusting out like the bill of some strange bird.
I had come to the conclusion that he had dropped asleep, and
indeed was nodding myself, when he suddenly sprang out of his
chair with the gesture of a man who has made up his mind and put
his pipe down upon the mantelpiece.

"Sarasate plays at the St. James's Hall this afternoon," he
remarked. "What do you think, Watson? Could your patients spare
you for a few hours?"

"I have nothing to do to-day. My practice is never very
absorbing."

We started off at once, and I accompanied my friend in his
drive. It was a glorious autumn afternoon, and the streets were
gay with a crowd enjoying the fine weather. The pavements were
thronged with pedestrians, and the roadway was alive with
vehicles of every description. Holmes drove in his usual reckless
fashion, and I felt that it was as well that he did not have to
do much pedestrian work, for his eyes and his thoughts were far
away, and his mind entirely preoccupied.

We walked along Strand, Holmes talking eagerly about the
programme, while I listened with a tolerant smile.  His mind, I
knew, was not on the music, but on the curious problem which he
had set himself to unravel.  His occasional glances towards
shops and side streets suggested that our destination was not the
concert hall, but some less predictable location.  I let him lead
me, content to wait and observe the workings of his brilliant and
eccentric mind.

We started off, therefore, for Saxe-Coburg Square, Mr. Holmes
carrying his ever-present deerstalker hat, and I my umbrella.  The
crisp autumn air was invigorating, and the bustling streets of
London held a certain charm even on this errand of investigation.  Holmes walked with a brisk, purposeful stride, his mind clearly
already engaged with the puzzle at hand, his keen eyes missing
nothing as we went.
We walked along the Strand, and Holmes led me through a maze of
narrow streets and alleys until we reached Saxe-Coburg Square.
The building was a rather imposing three story structure, with a
few shops on the ground floor and what seemed to be residential
units above.  He paused, looking up at the building, and then
pointed to a particular window on the second floor.

"That," he declared, "is the window of Mr. Jabez Wilson's office."
We started off for the City, Holmes in a mood of extreme
excitement, which showed itself in his alert eyes and fidgety
manner. As we walked I recounted to him the whole of Mr. Jabez
Wilson's statement, and he listened with the keenest attention. He
made no remarks except to ask the precise details of the house in
Coburg Square, where Wilson conducted his business, and to point
out the singular coincidence that the missing Duncan Ross should
have rented his room at the address given by the advertisement.

We travelled by the Underground as far as Aldersgate; and a short
walk took us to Saxe-Coburg Square, the scene of the singular
story which we had listened to in the morning. It was a poky,
little, shabby-genteel place, where four lines of dingy
two-storied brick houses looked out into a small railed-in
enclosure, where a lawn of weedy grass and a few clumps of faded
laurel-bushes made a hard fight against a smoke-laden and
uncongenial atmosphere. Three gilt balls and a brown board with
"JABEZ WILSON" in white letters, upon a corner house, announced
the place where our red-headed client carried on his business.
Sherlock Holmes stopped in front of it with his head on one side
and looked it all over, with his eyes shining brightly between
puckered lids. Then he walked slowly up the street, and then down
again to the corner, still looking keenly at the houses. Finally
he returned to the pawnbroker's, and, having thumped vigorously
upon the pavement with his stick two or three times, he went up
to the door and knocked. It was instantly opened by a
bright-looking, clean-shaven young fellow, who asked him to step
in.

"Thank you," said Holmes, "I only wished to ask you how you would
go from here to the Strand."

"Third right, fourth left," answered the assistant promptly,
closing the door.

The road in front of the pawnbroker's was a very quiet one, and
the detective's sharp eyes did not fail to notice every detail
which was presented to them. A small, dark street, almost
entirely composed of wooden buildings, stretched from the end of
Saxe-Coburg Square to the main road, and a low-lying building of
two floors was the only place of any kind in this side street.
Across the wooden structures on the other side were several small
squares which formed a pleasant contrast to the dinginess of
Saxe-Coburg Square.  Holmes scrutinized the houses with the air
of a connoisseur, and his eyes rested more than once upon the
low-lying house which had caught my attention.

The road in front of the pawnbroker's shop was a very narrow one,
and the pavement was so narrow that two persons could not pass
without great difficulty. The houses were all old and in bad
repair, and the whole neighbourhood was squalid and neglected. We
turned down a narrow passage which ran between two buildings and
which ended in a small yard at the back of the houses. It was
littered with refuse and rubble, and was evidently used as a
dust-bin. Two or three windows opened out upon the yard, and we
saw several rough-looking men in their shirtsleeves who were
engaged in some kind of work.

"That is where they are," said Holmes as we watched the
workmen.  "And now let us approach this matter from another
angle. We shall begin our inquiry from the other end."

The road in front of the pawnbroker's was a quiet one, but a few
yards to the south it became very lively, the houses giving place
to a row of shops, which were as active and bustling as the square
was stagnant. Holmes looked keenly at the numberings of the
houses and then at the various shops. Finally, he led the way
down a narrow passage, and then turned into a yard, where we
found a very dilapidated building, with some dirty windows.

"This is where the game is played," he remarked as he examined a
notice over the entrance.

The road in front of the pawnbroker's led to a yard which was
littered with debris.  Beyond the yard was a high brick wall,
which formed the boundary of the premises behind.  This wall was
of considerable height, and it was pierced by a single door, which
was heavily barred.  Holmes examined this door with the greatest
care, and then, after some searching amongst the rubbish, he
extracted a small rusty key from amongst a pile of old iron.  With
this key he carefully opened the door and turned the handle.

"Now, Watson," he whispered, "a little less noise. The game's
afoot."

The road which we took was flanked with a line of grimy workshops,
the most prominent of which was a large plasterer's. Opposite to
this was a small yard with a single door leading into it. As we
approached the yard the sound of hammering was heard from within,
and Holmes' quick eye caught the glint of a light shining
through a crack between the door and the doorpost. "That's our
man," said he, "and that is his work. It is our business to be
present when he finishes it." We took up our stand a little way
off, and watched the building.

The road in which we found ourselves as we turned round the
corner from the retired Saxe-Coburg Square presented as great a
contrast to it as the front of a picture does to the back. It was
one of the main arteries which conveyed the traffic of the City
to the north and west. The roadway was blocked with the immense
stream of commerce flowing in a double tide inward and outward,
while the footpaths were black with the hurrying swarm of
pedestrians. It was difficult to realise as we looked at the line
of fine shops and stately business premises that they really
abutted on the other side upon the faded and stagnant square
which we had just quitted.

We did as he suggested, and I must confess that the concert was
to me the best part of the day's adventures.  Holmes, however,
seemed to be more concerned with the programme than with the
performance, and several times I observed him studying it with
the greatest attention, while the violinist was in the midst of
one of his most brilliant passages.  It was only when the music
had ceased and the audience had risen that he finally satisfied
himself.  

"Now, Watson," he said, "we have heard the music, let's see what
the result may be!"

We did as he suggested, and spent a pleasant afternoon at the
concert, though I must confess that my thoughts were more
occupied with the singular problem which had been submitted to us
in the morning than with the performance of the Hungarian
virtuoso.  Holmes, however, was in one of his lighter moods, and
his conversation was as bright and sparkling as the music which we
were listening to.  He made several whimsical remarks about the
peculiarities of red-haired people, and once or twice he chuckled
to himself, as if he had some private joke which was beyond my
comprehension.

We lunched at a small Italian restaurant, and afterwards we
continued our journey to St. James's Hall, where we found plenty of
seats and spent a pleasant afternoon over the music. Holmes was
in one of his brighter moods, and he amused me by telling me of
some of his experiences with other red-headed people, and of the
curious inferences which he had drawn from the colour of their
hair. He finished with a dissertation on the many different
shades of colour, showing how they varied from the fiery orange of
the carrot to the dull brick dust of the setting sun, and how
many were the intermediate hues. As we came out of the hall he
turned his steps once more into the City, and we stopped at a
small pawnbroker's shop in the Tottenham Court Road.

"This is where our friend Mr. Jabez Wilson has had most of his
business dealings," said Holmes. "We may learn something
interesting by going in for half-an-hour. You will see."


We lunched at a small Italian restaurant, and afterwards we
hired a hansom and drove to St. James's Hall. The concert was
already in progress when we arrived. The hall was crowded, but
Holmes’s ingenious plan of getting into the front row had been
successful, and we had excellent seats just behind the
orchestra. For an hour and a half we listened, or rather, I
listened, for Holmes’s attention was wholly absorbed by the
musical performance. When the concert was over, he had the same
absorbed and dreamy expression on his face as he had shown
previously in his chair at home.

“Well, Watson,” he remarked as we went out into the bright
streets, “that was an exhilarating performance. How easily one
passes from the commonplace and dull to the sublime and noble,
from dull business to a scene of such great artistic merit!”

“And what has the concert to do with the case of the Red-headed
League?” I asked rather peevishly.

“A great deal, as it happens,” replied Holmes. “The little
assistant of Mr. Jabez Wilson has shown himself to be both
clever and daring. We can expect to find him equally
resourceful. If so, where could he find a safer and quieter place
to hide than at that concert? We know that he had a camera and
developing apparatus. That is a very clever line of action and
indicates a certain degree of shrewdness and resourcefulness. I
think we should call on him now.”

We had an excellent luncheon at a small Italian restaurant, and
afterwards we proceeded to St. James's Hall, where we had good
seats and listened with pleasure to the programme of the
afternoon. Holmes was in excellent spirits, and talked as we went
of the singular case which we had on hand.

"I am strongly inclined," said he, "to believe that this
conspiracy is connected with the business of the City and Suburban
Bank. Vincent Spaulding, you see, has a certain amount of
intelligence, and his presence in Saxe-Coburg Square is no mere
coincidence. They have cleverly managed to use a red-headed man
as a blind. But the object and the method are both shrouded in
mystery. It is a case where we should pause to consider the
method rather than the object."

"But the object must be the thing which interests us most."

"Most decidedly so. But I am bound to confess that at present
I am almost equally in the dark about both. But we shall have
more light this evening, Watson. We are going to Saxe-Coburg
Square again, to see Mr. Jabez Wilson, and after that we shall
probably call upon Mr. Duncan Ross, if we can find him. Meanwhile,
let us listen to the music."

My friend was an enthusiastic musician, being himself not only a
very capable performer but a composer of no ordinary merit. All
the afternoon he sat in the stalls wrapped in the most perfect
happiness, gently waving his long, thin fingers in time to the
music, while his gently smiling face and his languid, dreamy eyes
were as unlike those of Holmes the sleuth-hound, Holmes the
relentless, keen-witted, ready-handed criminal agent, as it was
possible to conceive. In his singular character the dual nature
alternately asserted itself, and his extreme exactness and
astuteness represented, as I have often thought, the reaction
against the poetic and contemplative mood which occasionally
predominated in him. The swing of his nature took him from
extreme languor to devouring energy; and, as I knew well, he was
never so truly formidable as when, for days on end, he had been
lounging in his armchair amid his improvisations and his
black-letter editions. Then it was that the lust of the chase
would suddenly come upon him, and that his brilliant reasoning
power would rise to the level of intuition, until those who were
unacquainted with his methods would look askance at him as on a
man whose knowledge was not that of other mortals. When I saw him
that afternoon so enwrapped in the music at St. James's Hall I
felt that an evil time might be coming upon those whom he had set
himself to hunt down.

"You want to go home, no doubt, Doctor," he remarked as we
emerged.

"Yes, it would be as well."

"And I have some business to do which will take some hours. This
business at Coburg Square is serious."

"Why serious?"

"A considerable crime is in contemplation. I have every reason to
believe that we shall be in time to stop it. But to-day being
Saturday rather complicates matters. I shall want your help
to-night."

"At what time?"

"Ten will be early enough."

"I shall be at Baker Street at ten."

I reached Baker Street a little before ten. Holmes was already
there, and was pacing rapidly up and down the room with his hands
in his pockets and an expression of the utmost excitement upon
his face. "This is a most extraordinary case, Watson," said he,
"and one which presented some curious features. I have all the
facts of Mr. Jabez Wilson's case laid out in front of me, and I
think I can deduce what occurred."

"Pray, let me hear your deductions."

"Good! Then listen carefully. In the first place, it is obvious
that this Red-headed League, with its apparently nonsensical
object of providing pay for red-haired men to copy out the
'Encyclopaedia Britannica,' was an elaborate scheme. Its
ostensible purpose was to mask the real purpose, which, of course,
was criminal."

"And what was that?"

"My dear Watson, this is the most difficult part of the business.
But if I am not mistaken, we shall very soon be in possession of
the true solution of the whole matter."
I confess that I was considerably startled by this last remark.
Holmes had never before spoken to me of danger in connection with
our investigations, and the very casual way in which he had
thrown off the suggestion seemed to indicate that it was a
serious one. I was glad to have my revolver with me, and I
found myself feeling a certain amount of excitement as I
journeyed back to my rooms, and thence to Baker Street.

I confess that I was considerably startled by this last remark,
though Holmes's habit of preparing for emergencies, and his
ever-present readiness for action, had long ceased to surprise
me. I reached home, ate my supper, and spent the evening with
my medical books, but I had not the same interest in my reading
as usual, for my mind was busy with the strange situation in which
I found myself. The problem which Holmes had set himself to solve
was certainly a most singular one, and it was evident that some
unusual combination of events and circumstances must have
conspired together to make it such. It was not, however, until
nearly ten o'clock that I found myself at Baker Street.

I reached Baker Street a little before ten, and I found Holmes
already waiting for me. He was dressed in a complete suit of
dark grey, with a black hat and gloves, and his expression was
such as I had never before seen upon his face. He seemed to be
struggling with some overpowering emotion which set his features
all aquiver, and his face was so pale and drawn that I feared that
he might be ill. "My dear Watson," he said in a voice which was
both eager and unsteady, "I am very sorry to bring you out on such
an errand, especially as it is a Saturday night and you might
wish to be spending it in a more cheerful way. But it is an
urgent and a vital matter, and it is one which will, I think,
interest you to the same degree as myself. It is of the utmost
importance that we should reach Saxe-Coburg Square by a quarter
past ten. We can get there by a cab, but we must hurry, for not
a second must be lost, and if we have to run we must run hard.
And now, Doctor, let us be off!"

I reached Baker Street a little before ten o'clock. Holmes was
already at the door waiting for me, his face pale and excited,
his eyes gleaming with eagerness.

"I've had a wire from the City and Suburban Bank," he said as we
started off together.  "Something important is happening."

I trust that I am not more dense than my neighbours, but I was
always oppressed with a sense of my own stupidity in my dealings
with Sherlock Holmes. Here I had heard what he had heard, I had
seen what he had seen, and yet from his words it was evident that
he saw clearly not only what had happened but what was about to
happen, while to me the whole business was still confused and
grotesque. As I drove home to my house in Kensington I thought
over it all, from the extraordinary story of the red-headed
copier of the "Encyclopaedia" down to the visit to Saxe-Coburg
Square, and the ominous words with which he had parted from me.
What was this nocturnal expedition, and why should I go armed?
Where were we going, and what were we to do? I had the hint from
Holmes that this smooth-faced pawnbroker's assistant was a
formidable man--a man who might play a deep game. I tried to
puzzle it out, but gave it up in despair and set the matter aside
until night should bring an explanation.

"Ha, Watson, you are just in time," cried Holmes. "This is
Inspector Baynes, of Scotland Yard, and Mr. Merryweather, who is
the chairman of the board of the City and Suburban Bank. You may
have heard the name. We have had a busy afternoon together."

"I have heard of the City and Suburban Bank," said I. "I am
somewhat familiar with its manager, Mr. John Clay."

"Ah, yes, Mr. John Clay," said Inspector Baynes, with a slight
shake of the head. "He is a worthy gentleman indeed. A rather
bad character, I should say, but he has never done anything which
would actually enable me to take action. I am very sorry that
we cannot have some evidence against him. This is a most
delicate business."

"I could not possibly be more anxious to help than I am," said
the respectable Mr. Merryweather. "I have no doubt that you are
familiar with the circumstances of the case. I will let you
know how it stands now. The City and Suburban Bank has always
been a thoroughly honest, respectable place. I have been the
chairman of the board for three years. The bank itself has been
in existence for some eighty years, and has had no scandal,
nothing to stain its fair repute, until now, in the present
horrible business."

"Horrible indeed!" I ejaculated.

"The worst that could possibly happen has occurred. It is an
absolutely unfathomable affair. The thieves have done what they
wanted, and left things just as they were. They have taken their
spoils and gone."

"So I understand," said Holmes. "But we are about to make them
disgorge their gains."

"You hope so, Mr. Holmes," said Mr. Merryweather, with a smile.
"I should have given it up. But if there is any possibility at
all it is only to be found in your wonderful skill."

"We shall make our attempt at ten o'clock," said Holmes to the
Inspector. "In the meantime Inspector, you would no doubt like to
rest."

"I propose to do so," said the Inspector, with a yawn.

"We shall have a cab at the door to convey ourselves to the spot,"
said Holmes to Mr. Merryweather.

"Then we will go into the next room," said Mr. Merryweather.
"I need some refreshment. I have not had a bite of food since
breakfast."

"Come, Watson," said Holmes; "I have told you that it is a three
pipe problem. Well, then, it is a three pipe problem, and I must
have my evening pipe now before we start upon our more serious
work."

"Ha! Our party is complete," cried Holmes, buttoning up his pea-
jacket and taking his deerstalker cap from the rack. "Jones, you
know Mr. Merryweather, the bank director, and this is my friend,
Dr. Watson."

The sad-faced gentleman bowed, and Mr. Jones, who was a
sturdy, middle-sized fellow, with a humorous, under-done
expression, nodded to me in a genial fashion.

"I think that we are all ready," said Holmes. "It is a quarter to
ten. Then we must go."

"Where to, sir?" I asked.

"To the City and Suburban Bank, in Queen Victoria Street. The
manager is our man. We shall be lucky if we arrive before
eleven."

"There is no mystery," I remarked, "about this visit to the
bank."

"No, none at all. It is perfectly clear now what is going on. That
is why I wish you to come. The thing has been so clear to me all
along that I am rather annoyed that I did not express myself
more lucidly. But it was so unusual a case that it might have
been difficult for you to follow it, even had I been more
explicit."

"Well, let us hear your reasons," said Jones. "I am, as I
need hardly say, most eager to be able to prevent the felony.
I would rather do that than make a dozen captures."

"Then you shall have it all," replied Holmes; "for it would,
indeed, be an immense relief to me. But you will find that my
reasons are very clear. First, then, is the fact that the Red-
headed League is a fraud. That is clear."

"Certainly," said Jones.

"And the bank will not need to be concerned."

"That is also clear."

"And I know, also, what the criminals really want."

"Ah!" cried both the others.

"It is what makes our job very dangerous."

"We are talking in riddles," said Jones, smiling.

"I am quite prepared to speak clearly," replied Holmes.  "I want
you to understand exactly what is about to happen.  We must leave
this street at once. I have my reasons."

"Ha! our party is complete," said Holmes, buttoning up his pea-jacket and taking his deerstalker cap from the rack.  "Jones, you have heard of the matter?  Good.  Now, Mr. Merryweather, let me introduce you to my friend, Dr. Watson, who is occasionally good enough to assist me in my little affairs.  You are aware that this is a serious business."
"Ha, Watson, you are just in time," cried Holmes cheerily. "I
have here two gentlemen who desire to hear the explanation of
the singular affair of the Red-headed League. Meet Mr. Merryweather,
bank director, and Mr. Jones, who is the very able detective
from Scotland Yard." The two officials bowed, and Mr. Merryweather
a stout man with a pompous air, made a little speech which was
somewhat marred by a nervous tremor in his voice.

"Ha! our party is complete," cried Holmes, but his voice was not
the voice of the Holmes whom I had known. It was sharp and
irritable. "You are late, Doctor. Mr. Merryweather, I presume
this is your friend?"

The sad-faced gentleman gave a very frigid nod, and I saw by the
light of the lamp that his face was composed of hard, sharp
angles.

"Pray, gentlemen," said Holmes, "to what do I owe this honour?
And, perhaps, you would kindly tell me why you have chosen this
most inappropriate hour for your visit. It is midnight or near
it."

"Mr. Sherlock Holmes," said Jones, stepping forward, "we owe you
an apology. I can only say that this matter was immediately
placed in my hands, and that I have been working on it almost
constantly since you first took it up. I had not, however,
succeeded in tracing it to its sources until late this afternoon.
You may know that it has been rumoured amongst the force that you
are a man of exceptional ability, and I have no doubt that this
will give you every reason to think so. Our theory is that the
Red-headed League is connected with the City and Suburban Bank.
Mr. Merryweather, here, is the chief accountant of that bank, and
his suspicions were aroused by the events connected with this
very singular case."

"I will explain to you the exact facts of the case," said Mr.
Merryweather. "Yesterday evening, after the bank was closed, one
of the clerks--a Mr. Spaulding, who, it seems, is the assistant
of Jabez Wilson--remained to put some entries in a particular
ledger. It had been a busy day and he worked until nearly
midnight. When he left, Mr. Spaulding bolted the door, and
returned to his house in Saxe-Coburg Square."


"Ha! Our party is complete," said Holmes, buttoning up his
pea-jacket and taking his heavy hunting crop from the rack.
"Watson, I think you know Mr. Jones, of Scotland Yard? Let me
introduce you to Mr. Merryweather, who is to be our companion in
to-night's adventure."

"You've seen the advertisement of the League, have you not?" asked
Sherlock Holmes.

"Yes," answered Mr. Merryweather. "It was I who caused the
insertion."

"Then you were kind enough to call this morning?"

"I was," said Mr. Merryweather. "My visit was, I must confess,
of a somewhat unusual nature, and yet I am not altogether
unprepared for the possibility that you have already guessed
what it was."

"We have reached that point," said Holmes. "Our little game is
played out."

"And what is the result, pray?"

"I'll tell you," said Holmes. "Mr. Jabez Wilson's case is, I
find, a very singular one, and it does not quite conform to the
expectations that one would have formed from what one knows of
him. The idea of the League is certainly novel. The way in which
this eccentric Mr. Hopkins bequeathed his fortune for the benefit
of all red-headed men is certainly peculiar, and that a considerable
amount of money should have been laid out in the enterprise is
also peculiar. But it is, as Mr. Merryweather says, exceedingly
strange that this elaborate scheme should have been used in order
to get information concerning the whereabouts of the private
premises of a firm of brokers. There is something very unusual
about the whole affair, and yet the more I consider it the more
I see that the only unusual thing about it is that it has not
happened many hundreds of times before. That is what makes the
whole thing so extraordinary. What is it that makes you so
unhappy about this case?"

"You are, perhaps, aware that this is the private office of the
City and Suburban Bank?"

"Yes, indeed, Mr. Merryweather. It is quite clear that I cannot
tell you how I know that."

"That is what is puzzling me," he cried. "There is not much
to be learned by examining this room. This is simply the
private office of the bank manager, and we don't want to
make a commotion by breaking in."

"No, surely not," said Holmes. "The object is not to break in,
but to go in. There is a difference, however. We do not wish to
deprive the bank manager of his private office; but we want to
find out what is contained within it."

"As I understand, Mr. Merryweather, you wish to know whether
this is not more than an accident."

"Yes, I wish to find out whether we are not on the verge of a
considerable disaster."

"Then we must go now, for it is past ten."

"Then let us start," said Mr. Merryweather. "I have my own
key."

"And my revolver," said I.

"I do not wish to seem to intrude," remarked Mr. Jones of
Scotland Yard. "But I may say that I have received my
instructions from the authorities, and that we are going this
way with you."

Holmes smiled gravely. "Your presence has been expected, Mr. Jones.
Shall we proceed?"

"You will find it as serious as it is strange," said Holmes, "but
I beg that you will leave the whole thing in my hands. I have
already formed my conclusions, and if you will act precisely
upon my directions you will find that all will turn out well. I
shall only ask you to follow me without question, and to act
exactly as I bid you."

"You may place considerable confidence in Mr. Holmes, sir," said
Jones. "He is a man who is never at fault."

"Oh, yes, I know," said Merryweather, "but still—"

"It is only a question of keeping to time," remarked Holmes; "our
main business is a matter of five minutes past ten. Do you think
you could manage to be ready at that hour, Mr. Merryweather?"

"Certainly," said he. "But it is surely unnecessary to take all
this elaborate precaution."

"Not at all," replied Holmes; "the more elaborate the precautions
the less the danger. It's merely elementary."

"Well, I have never known such elaborate preparations made for
anything," said Merryweather. "I have gone armed to the teeth on
many an occasion, but I never remember such a careful display of
forethought and preparation as this."

"That's what makes my business so exciting," Holmes remarked,
as we drove to our destination.

"You'll find it none the less exciting on that account," Holmes
answered with a laugh. "At present we are only just at the
beginning of this adventure. However, as you are both very
familiar with the situation, there is no need for me to make any
detailed statement of the case. I wish you simply to follow my
instructions implicitly and to act exactly as I bid you. Do you
agree to that?"

Both men signified their agreement.

"You may place considerable confidence in Mr. Holmes, sir," said
the police agent loftily. "He has his own little methods, which
are, if he will excuse my saying so, just a little too
unconventional for the tastes of a practical man. But he has
results, Mr. Merryweather, he has results."

"I should hope so, indeed," said Holmes with a dry smile, and he
led us down to the street. The two hansoms were still there, and
as we entered them I observed that Mr. Merryweather was
carrying a small leather bag, which he placed at his feet.

"You may place considerable confidence in Mr. Holmes, sir," said
the police agent loftily. "He has his own little methods, which
are, if he won't mind my saying so, just a little too theoretical
and fantastic, but he has the makings of a detective in him. It
is not too much to say that once or twice, as in that business of
the Sholto murder and the Agra treasure, he has been more nearly
correct than the official force."

"I trust that you will find this investigation more exciting,"
said Holmes.  "And I am sure that you will not regret this
opportunity of making the acquaintance of Mr. Jabez Wilson, of
Coburg Square."  The mention of our red-headed client brought a
look of surprise into the features of the respectable Mr.
Merryweather.
"I know, my dear Mr. Merryweather; but compare your loss with
the situation.  Think of the millions which are at stake!  This
is bigger than a rubber of whist.  Shall we start?" Holmes
asked, briskly.

"I think we can manage without you to-night, Mr. Merryweather,"
said Holmes drily. "Our little problem should be solved by
eleven. And now, gentlemen, are you both ready? Then let us
start at once, for time presses."

"I think we can dispense with our usual game to-night, Mr.
Merryweather," said Holmes. "Perhaps you would prefer to play for
a higher stake than your usual one. And now, gentlemen, we have
at most an hour before we can get to work. Let us spend it in
pleasantries. Let us talk of hobbies. Is there any hobby, Mr.
Merryweather, in which you find consolation?"

"Yes, sir," answered Merryweather, "I am an expert in bric-à-brac,
but I would rather talk about the matter which has brought us
together to-night. What do you expect us to do?"

"To call upon Mr. Vincent Spaulding, the amiable assistant of
Mr. Jabez Wilson," said Holmes.


"I expect that you are aware, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes, "that
I have some small reputation with the police, and that they rate
my assistance as being occasionally of value. They are very
good people, the police, but they are not very bright."

"Just so," said Mr. Merryweather dryly. "It is, as you say, most
important to keep this matter quiet. The less said about it the
better."

"I think you will find," said Sherlock Holmes, "that you will
play for a higher stake to-night than you have ever done yet, and
that the play will be more exciting. For you, Mr. Merryweather,
the stake will be some 30,000 pounds; and for you, Jones, it will
be the man upon whom you wish to lay your hands."

"I hope that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to him
to-night," said Holmes with a smile. "I have had one or two
previous meetings with him which led to nothing very serious, but
I am hopeful that to-night may be more fortunate. As to you, Mr.
Merryweather, you will look on upon the scene, while Jones and I
act. I have, as you know, little faith in the methods of
official investigation; but I have always found that they are
useful when one wants to secure a man."

"I hope that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to him
to-night," said Holmes. "This adventure promises to be more
exciting than the hunt for the Baskerville hound, and at least
as complex as the case of the noble bachelor."  He chuckled, and
then, taking a square and bulky envelope from his desk, he opened
it and revealed to us a number of short, crisp newspaper cuttings
all relating to the singular case of the Red-headed League.

"I have here, my friends," said he, "the whole history of the
business." He drew his chair closer and began to narrate the
events from the point where he had taken the case up.

"The details of Mr. Jabez Wilson's singular adventure," said he,
"are extremely curious, but, really, they are quite commonplace
when one considers them carefully. A red-headed man was
needed. Vincent Spaulding, my client's remarkably energetic
assistant, was not too far removed from being a red-head. With a
vigorous use of hair dye he assumed the role, and applied for the
vacancy which was clearly marked for him."

"I hope that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to him
to-night," said Holmes. "I have reason to believe that he will be
waiting for us."

"Then, it is time we were off," said Jones.

"Not yet, Jones," Holmes answered. "You must complete your
preparations. I have something here which may be useful to you."

He handed Jones a small, flat, oblong tin. Jones opened it and
displayed a curious collection of squares of coloured paper.

"These are signals," said Holmes. "With these we can show the
direction which he has taken. We shall make our way to the
City and Suburban Bank. Do you know it?"

"Yes, I know it well," answered Mr. Merryweather. "I have to
visit it at this hour every Saturday on business of the bank."

"Then you know the back way through the yard? Good. It is
essential that we should be there before our friend."

"Let us go then," said Mr. Merryweather.

"Not yet," Holmes answered. "It is the last stroke of the clock
which is required to begin the performance."

"I hope that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to him
to-night," said Holmes. "This pawnbroker's assistant, Mr.
Spaulding, is none other than John Clay, who we know has had
something to do with a number of crimes, and whose arrest will be
no small matter to the police.  We are just going to Saxe-Coburg
Square. I thought that it would be as well if you were to be
there in case our theories prove to be correct. You had best
wait outside until I give a signal."

"I hope that we may be more fortunate to-night," said Holmes.
"Mr. Merryweather, I understand that you are going to the City
and Suburban Bank?"

"Yes, sir. And I wish I may get through the night without
trouble."

"Well, you must have a good deal of trouble if you get involved in
the case of young John Clay," said Jones, with a chuckle, "for I
don't know anyone who is more anxious to meet him than I am. But
we are quite ready to start when you are, Mr. Holmes."

"I hope that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to-night.
I've had one or two little turns also with Mr. John Clay, and I
agree with you that he is at the head of his profession. It is
past ten, however, and quite time that we started. If you two
will take the first hansom, Watson and I will follow in the
second."

"This is where we leave our hansoms," said Holmes getting out and
paying the driver. "We shall walk the rest of the way."

"This is where we leave the hansom," said Holmes. "We have a
little walk before us, Watson, and a rather serious one. I trust
that you are in good condition."

"I have not had much exercise of late, and am feeling rather
tired."

"The less you say the better, and the more you listen the
better. We shall have a silent walk for about a quarter of an
hour. Now, then, let us begin."

"We are close there," said Holmes. "This is the City and Suburban
Bank. That's the place. You see that dark doorway? That is where
we go in."

"We are close there," said Holmes, pointing to a massive
building which towered up above the others like a giant. "That is
the City and Suburban Bank. It was there that the deed which we
are to witness was done. This is what we have to do. You,
Mr. Jones, are to wait here with your assistant, and when I
give a signal you are to rush in and arrest John Clay. Mr.
Merryweather will remain with me. This is a great thing for the
bank, and we must be discreet. We are going in by the side door,
so that we may not be seen."

"This is where we leave the cabs," said Holmes, getting out and
paying the driver. "It is a quarter to eleven. We shall have
plenty of time. Now, Mr. Merryweather, I should be glad if you
would go on to the office alone. You should find the manager there.
It would not be wise for us to appear. You will see the need in
a few minutes. Meanwhile, Watson and I will await you here."

"We are close there now," my friend remarked. "This fellow
Merryweather is a bank director, and personally interested in the
matter. I thought it as well to have Jones with us also. He is
not a bad fellow, though an absolute imbecile in his profession.
He has one positive virtue. He is as brave as a bulldog and as
tenacious as a lobster if he gets his claws upon anyone. Here we
are, and they are waiting for us."

"Yes, it is a curious thing," said Holmes, peering about with his
lantern.  "And I perceive that the cellar extends considerably
farther back than one would have supposed. There is another
door there behind the boxes. I wonder what that leads to?"

"It is rather an interesting point," said Holmes. "It appears to
be a very strong vault. I presume that you have not any very
strong boxes here?"

"All our strong boxes are on the upper floors."

"How many people work in this vault?"

"At present, only my secretary and myself."

"And your secretary?"

"He is the only other person who possesses a key."

"What is his name?"

"Vincent Spaulding."

A gasp of astonishment escaped from Holmes' lips and he turned
pale. "Vincent Spaulding!" he cried. "But it is impossible!"

"I could not possibly have said it better," remarked Mr.
Merryweather dryly. "The man is the only other person who has a
key, and he is about as dangerous a customer as London holds. This
is his masterpiece."

"I must really ask you to be more careful," said Holmes severely.
"You have already told us too much."  Mr. Merryweather opened his
mouth to reply, but Holmes silenced him with a look.  "Now, Mr.
Jones," he continued, "it is time for you to play your part."

"Yes," said Holmes, turning to his companion, "there is a
considerable space between the ceiling of this vault and the
floor of the bank above. We must be careful not to disturb the
quiet of the night. It may interest you to learn that our friend
John Clay has never done a piece of work which has been more
audacious than this. You may say that his skill is equal to his
courage. When you consider that the vaults of this bank are lined
with steel two feet in thickness, that the outer doors have not
only been locked, but have also been sealed, and bolted from
the inside, and that the space between the bank and the cellars
is too small to allow a man to crawl through, you will admit
that the feat is a very remarkable one."

"It's a fine thing for the bank," said the police agent, "that
you have come to our help, Mr. Holmes. I confess that it was a
most puzzling affair."

"I have only one thing to ask," said Holmes: "Let me have a
few words with Mr. Jabez Wilson before we start."

"What!"

"Yes; he may have a clue, which, added to what we know, will be
of immense service."

"I shall certainly go over the case with him if you think that it
would be of any service to us."

"Well, then," said Holmes, "let us wait until we have actually
found the criminal, for the solution will then be much clearer."

"Very good," said Mr. Merryweather. "Now, with your permission,
gentlemen, we will proceed to our business."

"I ask you to observe that I am carrying neither arms nor
anything in my hands," said Holmes as he moved forward. "It is
absolutely necessary that our approach should be silent."

"It is certainly not solid," said Holmes, tapping with his
cane. "There are several passages here besides this one, I
imagine?"

"Yes, indeed," the bank director answered, "this place is
honeycombed with little passages, which open into the main
sewers of London. They are an infernal nuisance, and we are
constantly finding that our boxes are being undermined, and
our treasure is being gradually oozed away from under our
very feet."

"Perhaps it is John Clay who is doing the undermining?" I remarked.

"I should think it very likely," said Merryweather. "It's a
remarkably clever thing, though, is it not? It looks as if we
should never get him."

"I have come to learn something, however," said Holmes. "What is
the small building opposite?"

"That is my house," said Merryweather. "And now, gentlemen, I have
only to make one thing clear to you before we start. That small
building opposite is our bank. A tunnel leads from it into the
vault where we are standing. I have placed my agents on guard
there, and they will promptly arrest John Clay and his
associates should they attempt to use the passage."

"And what about your other agents?"

"All along the line in the cellars and tunnels. You see, we've
had a hint of what was going on. We found ourselves very insecure.
So we kept our eyes open."

"And your other tunnel?"

"That's the mystery," said Mr. Merryweather. "No tunnel has been
discovered."

"Yes, I should think not," said Holmes. "A tunnel in this way
might be stopped in a moment. A tunnel in the other way could
not be discovered until after the event. The bank director would
have no means of finding out."

"Indeed?"

"Yes, let us proceed."


"I must really ask you to be a little more quiet!" said Holmes
severely. "You have already imperilled the whole success of our
expedition. Might I beg that you would have the goodness to sit
down upon one of those boxes, and not to interfere?"

"Yes, it is a blind," said he; "but a very clever one. Beautifully
done, too!" He held up a little disc of metal. "This is what I
found stuck in the crack of the pavement. This little piece of
metal has no value in itself, but if you examine it carefully you
will see that it is a key."

"A key?"

"Exactly. This key has opened a lock. But we are going to open
it to-night, Mr. Merryweather. To-night we are going to open
it!"

"Yes, it is a blind alley," said he. "What do you mean by that?"
asked Merryweather. "We have no way out. That is what we mean by
calling it a blind alley. This is the end of the passage. And now
we are in the same position as the man who found the treasure
in the tale. We have only to find the way to get into it."

"But how is the treasure?" asked Jones.

"There is but one entrance," replied Holmes, "which is from the
office in Saxe-Coburg Square. Through that, the thieves have
entered."

"Then how can we catch them?" asked Jones.

"Let us see. The walls are strong on all sides. We can find no
other way out. Now let us trace this passage to its end."

"It's a blind alley!" shouted Merryweather.

"Exactly. A blind alley! And that is the reason why I have asked
you to come with me, Mr. Merryweather."

"Yes," said he, "it is perfectly clear. There are only two ways
into this cellar. One is through the door by which we entered,
and the other is through the trap-door in the floor. There is
no other way, and yet the man must have been here. Now we have to
think how he got in and how he got out."

"Yes," said he, "it would appear that there are worse dangers
than our friend from above. Mr. Merryweather, you may leave your
lanterns here. You also, Jones. Now, Watson, come with me."

"Yes," said he, "the ventilation is excellent; one of the best
that I have ever seen. I'm not sure that I have ever seen a better
one. What do you think of it, Watson?"

"It's a very good one," I answered.

"Indeed, it is perfect," said Holmes. "And now, gentlemen, for
the next step. The plans which I have laid are tolerably
complete. What they expect is that they will be able to get away
with the loot on a dark night and then vanish safely into the
crowd. I have an unpleasant surprise for them. I hope the
arrangements are quite clear?"

"Quite so," said Jones and Mr. Merryweather in unison.

"Then let us proceed to the business in hand, for there is, as
I understand, an exceedingly thin crust of earth between our
feet and our friends below."

"Then let us have it," said Jones, rubbing his hands with
glee.  "I have not had such a good hunt for a long time."

"Pray be seated," said Holmes, smiling.  "We have only to wait."

"We have at least an hour before us," he remarked, "for they can
hardly take any steps until the good pawnbroker is safely in bed.
Then they will not lose a minute, for the sooner they do their
work the longer time they will have for their escape. We are at
present, Doctor--as no doubt you have divined--in the cellar of
the City branch of one of the principal London banks. Mr.
Merryweather is the chairman of directors, and he will explain to
you that there are reasons why the more daring criminals of
London should take a considerable interest in this cellar at
present."

"It is our French gold," whispered the director. "We have had
several warnings that an attempt might be made upon it."

"Your French gold?"

"It is indeed a treasure well worth taking," remarked Holmes. "Well,
gentlemen, we can only wait now, but I hardly think that we shall
have long to wait."

He sat down on a box, and, closing his eyes, he began to
hum, a low, monotonous droning tune.  The only sounds in the
vast vault were the gentle breathing of the watchers and the
occasional drip of water from the rocky ceiling.  I myself felt
a creeping unease, despite Holmes's calm demeanor.  The air was
heavy, and the silence oppressive.

"If there were only some device," said Holmes, glancing keenly
at the vault, "by which we could instantly communicate with
the police when once these robbers had made their entrance,
then we could catch them red-handed, and that would be a
considerable triumph."

"But how could we communicate with them?"

"Good heavens, what is that?"

A sudden scraping of a match had startled us. It has been followed
by the flare of a dark lantern, which was swung to and fro in front
of our faces.

"It is singular," remarked Holmes, "that neither you nor your
directors ever attempted to ascertain what was actually in the
cellar. It is also singular that in all your warnings you never
mentioned the nature of the warnings you had received."

"Well, it was the opinion of several of the directors that the
warnings were not worth considering," said Mr. Merryweather, "and
the subject was dropped. I alone had misgivings; and, though I
had no definite information on which to act, I felt it my duty to
take every precaution. When Mr. Holmes came to me this morning, I
was greatly relieved to find that his plans were identical with
my own."

"Which were?"

"To make a thorough examination of the cellar."

"That's it," said Holmes.  "But it was certainly a curious
coincidence that you should have chosen this very day for the
examination."


"I understand," said Holmes. "And I understand also that you are
to be here to-night to protect the treasure?"

"Yes, sir. Jones here and myself, and two more of my colleagues."

"Excellent!" said Holmes. "And you are armed?"

"Yes, sir. We are four strong."

"Then the situation is really a very simple one," said Holmes,
chuckling. "It is merely a question of whether you can take John
Clay alive or whether he gets the start of you."

"Is he likely to come to-night?"

"I think it is certain."

"Why?"

"Because I have had the honour of an interview with him."

"The misgiving of the directors," observed Holmes, "was a very
justifiable one, and I very much fear that this unfortunate affair
will cause them considerable inconvenience. I must now ask you to
give me a description of your French gold, Mr. Merryweather."

"There are 30,000 napoleons," answered the banker; "each of them
value twenty francs, packed in one hundred and fifty packets of
two hundred each.  They are contained in sixty-five double-locked
cases."


"Which were very well justified," observed Holmes. "And now it is
time that we arranged our little plans. I expect that within an
hour matters will come to a head. In the meantime Mr.
Merryweather, we must put the screen over that dark lantern."

"And sit in the dark?"

I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case,
and took my position, with my eyes fixed upon the door. We were
all silent now, save for the occasional scratching of a rat
behind the boxes. The minutes seemed to drag into an eternity.
Holmes held his watch in his hand, and from time to time he would
whisper the time. I had a thousand conflicting thoughts, but my
revolver was ready for any emergency. The night was very
still, save for the low hum of the traffic outside.

I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case,
and took my position, with my heart beating like a drum. The
other two did as they had been told, and all was still once more
in the vault, save for the gentle breathing of the watchers. The
darkness was intense, and the silence was absolute.

The sounds of movement above had become more pronounced. We heard
the creaking of boards, and the scraping of a tool against stone.
Then there was a sudden hush, which lasted for a few seconds, and
then several distinct heavy blows, struck at intervals. Holmes
looked at his watch.

"It is coming on for midnight," he said. "Have you your pistols
ready? Jones, if you are not yourself in a position to do
anything further, I wish you would keep an eye on Mr. Merryweather here, for I have a suspicion that he is more easily startled
than he would have us believe."

"Very well, sir," said the police agent. "All right, sir."

"Keep your pistol well to the front, but be cautious not to use
it until I say so. And now, Mr. Merryweather, you will have the
goodness to let us have the lantern."

I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case
beside me, and took my position, with my eyes fixed upon the
dark opening which led to the street. The silence was only broken
by the occasional drip of water which fell with a sharp, sudden
sound from the ceiling into the pool at our feet. The darkness
was intense, and I knew that more than one pair of eyes besides
my own were fixed on the same point.

I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case,
and took my position, with my eyes upon the dark opening which
led up to the street. The silence was only broken by the gentle
drip, drip of water which fell from the roof and echoed in the
vast emptiness of the vault. Holmes moved about among the boxes,
the lantern casting strange shadows on the walls. Then, with a
sudden sharp clang, a sound which had nothing to do with the
dropping water, the gate of the cellar was flung open, and three
men entered, armed and masked.

"This is our chance!" whispered Holmes.

I placed my revolver, cocked, upon the top of the wooden case
behind which I crouched. Holmes shot the slide across the front
of his lantern and left us in pitch darkness--such an absolute
darkness as I have never before experienced. The smell of hot
metal remained to assure us that the light was still there, ready
to flash out at a moment's notice. To me, with my nerves worked
up to a pitch of expectancy, there was something depressing and
subduing in the sudden gloom, and in the cold dank air of the
vault.

"They have but one retreat," whispered Holmes. "That is back
through the house into Saxe-Coburg Square. I hope that you have
done what I asked you, Jones?"

"I have an inspector and two officers waiting at the front door."

"Then we have stopped all the holes. And now we must be silent
and wait."

It was a little, tiny, silvery point, no bigger than a star, but
it was enough to guide me. In an instant Holmes had snatched the
screen from the lantern. The light blazed out with dazzling
brightness, and the whole vault was illuminated. The scene which
met our eyes was an extraordinary one. In the center of the
cellar there stood three figures. One was a tall, stout man, with
a florid face and a great red beard. It was Mr. Jabez Wilson, the
pawnbroker. He was standing as rigid and motionless as a statue,
with his eyes fixed upon the floor.

It was a little, tiny, pinpoint of light, but it was enough to
show me that a dark lantern was slowly and cautiously opening. I
gave a low whistle to warn my companions, and Holmes, in an
instant, had his hand on the lever. As the light came on, I
looked around at our comrades.

Their faces were shining with excitement. Jones was in his
element, ready for the tussle. Even Mr. Merryweather, the solemn
bank director, had his eyes gleaming with eagerness.

It was a very faint light, but it was there. It appeared and
disappeared spasmodically, as though someone were holding a
lantern and moving it up and down. Then it grew stronger and
stronger, and finally there was a sudden glare, and Holmes's voice
rang out: "Now, then! Stand back!"

It was very faint, and seemed to come from just beneath the
floorings. Then I saw a dark line along the edge of the boards
and then another, and another, and so on in a regular sequence
until they formed a kind of pattern of a line of squares all round
the room.  The squares were small, but a few minutes' watching
showed me that they were growing larger, and the line of them
was slowly receding.

It was a tiny, pinpoint of light, but it was enough to make my
heart beat. It grew larger, and then I saw the dark outline of a
man's head and shoulders against it. An instant later there was
a click, a sharp metallic sound, and the light vanished.

"Now then!" cried Holmes, and, seizing his lantern, he flashed
it full upon the spot.

At first it was but a lurid spark upon the stone pavement. Then
it lengthened out until it became a yellow line, and then,
without any warning or sound, a gash seemed to open and a hand
appeared, a white, almost womanly hand, which felt about in the
centre of the little area of light. For a minute or more the
hand, with its writhing fingers, protruded out of the floor. Then
it was withdrawn as suddenly as it appeared, and all was dark
again save the single lurid spark which marked a chink between
the stones.

A sudden flash of light from Holmes's lantern showed us the two
figures. The taller one, the red-haired, was the first to spring
out and make a dash for it. The other followed close behind. But
Mr. Merryweather had already grasped the red-headed one by the
collar and pulled him back, while Holmes promptly collared the
other.

"It's Vincent Spaulding, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes. "You
remember that name, don't you? And the other is John Clay, a man
who is wanted as much for forgery as for murder."

A chorus of shouts answered him, and a flash of light in the
darkness showed me the two figures as they sprang to their feet
and turned to run. Holmes dashed forward.  The smaller man, the
red-haired one, made a sudden movement as if to strike Holmes
down, but Holmes was too quick for him, and with a deft twist
had him firmly gripped by the collar and the throat.

Before Holmes could utter a word, the red-headed man on the floor
had sprung into the air, and we all rushed together at him. Jones
had the fellow by the collar almost before he had touched the
ground. Then there was a scramble, a shout, a scuffle, and then
as suddenly as it had begun the whole thing was over.

"Got him!" cried Jones triumphantly, holding him down with his
weight. "What, is he not a beauty? I haven't seen such a well-set-up
fellow since I had to deal with the great Biddlecomb Bank affair."

"Yes," said Holmes, dusting his knees and adjusting his coat.
"But his beauty will not save him."

"What is he then?" asked Mr. Merryweather. "A gentleman, is it?"

"A most typical case of the Red-Headed League," Holmes answered,
winking at me, "but of what value is the Red-Headed League
without its leader?"

"I'll take this one along to the police station," said Jones.
"What about your assistant, Mr. Wilson?"

"He's the real criminal, but we've got him now," answered Mr.
Merryweather cheerfully. "And the French gold too!"

A sudden flash of light from Holmes' lantern showed us the two
figures.  One, shorter and slighter, was indeed a vivid, almost
fiery red-head. The other, taller, was struggling to pull a heavy
sack from the hole.  Before either of them could make a move,
Holmes' powerful voice rang out.

A sudden flash from Holmes's lantern showed us the two figures as
they stood. At the same instant, Mr. Merryweather dashed
forward with a cry, and flung himself upon the shorter of the
two, while Holmes, with equal promptness, flung himself upon the
elder. The latter had drawn his revolver, but he fired too
quickly, and missed. Holmes had him by the collar and the
struggle was over instantly. The red-haired man, however, was a
wrestler of astonishing strength and, for a time, Holmes was
unable to throw him. He pressed his hand upon the man's mouth
to stop his cries, and held him in a grip which was like a
vise.

Sherlock Holmes had sprung out and seized the intruder by the
collar. The other dived down the hole, and I heard the sound of
rending cloth as Jones clutched at his skirts. The light flashed
upon the barrel of a revolver, but Holmes' hunting crop came
down on the man's wrist, and the pistol clinked upon the stone
floor.

"It's no use, John Clay," said Holmes blandly. "You have no
chance at all."

"So I see," the other answered with the utmost coolness. "I fancy
that my pal is all right, though I see you have got his
coat-tails."

"There are three men waiting for him at the door," said Holmes.

"Oh, indeed! You seem to have done the thing very completely. I
must compliment you."

"And I you," Holmes answered. "Your red-headed idea was very new
and effective."

"You'll see your pal again presently," said Jones. "He's quicker
at climbing down holes than I am. Just hold out while I fix the
derbies."

"Now, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes, "we must leave you to
congratulate yourself upon the recovery of your French gold.
Perhaps it would be as well if you sent your cashier round on
Monday morning to the office of the Red-headed League. It may
spare you some embarrassment."

"I have no doubt that he will do so," answered the director with
some sternness.  "I understand that you are going to Saxe-Coburg
Square?"


As he stepped across the threshold he gave one of his peculiar,
high-pitched, chuckling laughs. "It just shows you," he said,
"that even a Red-headed League can be useful sometimes." And then
he was gone.

"Now, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes, "we have only to make our
report to the police and to you, and then we will go to bed, for
I am sure that we have earned our rest."

"You will let me know, Mr. Holmes," said Merryweather, "if you
have any further light on the matter. It is quite inexplicable
to me."

"Explicable enough," said Holmes. "It was clearly the work of
John Clay and his accomplice. The former is one of the most
clever and daring criminals in England. His methods are quite
unique. It is always the unusual which attracts his attention.
The circumstances surrounding your French gold and the apparent
difficulty of getting at it would naturally give him a pleasing
sense of the unusual and make him look upon the whole thing as a
sporting proposition. The Red-headed League was merely a blind to
get him into the place and give him time to work. The assistant
whom you employed was his accomplice, and one of the cleverest
men in London. I shall have something to say presently about his
method of opening the doors and his presence among the red-heads.
What you really want to know, Mr. Merryweather, is how these
criminals knew about that French gold."

"Now, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes, turning to the bank
director, "we may consider that this little incident is closed.
We have saved the Bank of France some 30,000 napoleons, which is no
small matter. I have only just one question to put to you. One
of the men was taller than the other, and wore a frock-coat. Which
of them was it?"

"The taller one was Spaulding," answered Mr. Merryweather.

"And the other is Vincent Spaulding also."

"Vincent Spaulding!" said Holmes. "And it is this one that I know
so well, for I have known him for years. A curious coincidence,
that the man who had been of such use in this matter was
actually the same one whom I wanted in another affair. Well, it
is not easy to find a man's body in the Thames, or to prove
that it is the same man, but there is no doubt that it was
Spaulding, and not an impostor, who was working in my
neighbourhood."

"You seem to have a pretty good knowledge of John Clay's methods,"
I remarked.

"I know he has a particular fancy for doing his work upon a
Saturday night. I was not sure of my man till to-night. And now I
think we have earned a long rest."

"So long a rest, Holmes," I exclaimed, "that, before we do any
more night work, we'll have a pretty long nap at home."


"Now, Mr. Merryweather," said Holmes, "we have been successful,
thanks to this young man's most laudable enterprise. I can only
add that I do not think we should have been successful without
it. I confess, however, that I did not know what he was
thinking of when, in answer to my query as to where he lived, he
said that the direction was 'Third right, fourth left.' Now I
know. That was the route he must take to reach this place. That
was the point from which he came to-night. But what I do not
understand is why he took such a risk for so small a sum as a few
pounds a week."

"That was hardly the point, Mr. Holmes," said Merryweather. "That
was merely the bait. Of course, I have been in touch with this
business all along, for it was I who arranged for the
advertisement to appear in the Chronicle. I am very much
