indebted to you for your assistance, and though I have been quite
in the dark, I see now that a great danger lay behind this
seemingly trivial matter. However, we are all very much in your
debt."

"You may say so, sir," said Jones in a loud voice. "And it is not
every day that you have the chance of giving your advice to such
a wonderful man as Holmes here. I had heard of him, of course,
and of his methods, but when I saw him start off like this,
without knowing where he was going or what he was going to do, I
was pretty much amazed. The whole business looked pretty hopeless
to me, but when I see a man like Holmes taking the matter up
it gives me more hope."

"But why did your assistant do it?" I asked.

"Ah, that's the interesting point," said Holmes.

"I'll tell you," said Mr. Merryweather. "We had found that
something was going wrong at the bank and suspected a leak.
Spaulding was my cousin. I brought him in here to get a look at
the whole situation. I needed a man with a good knowledge of
London, capable and willing to be inconspicuous. He watched the
bank for weeks from Mr. Wilson's pawn shop. He took note of
everything and developed a plan to get inside the bank undetected,
using the red-haired League vacancy as a means. It was only a
small part of the plan--this whole League of Redheads scheme was
a diversion--but it was an important one."

"Quite so," said Holmes.  "I observed those rather shiny knees of
his.  A man who spends his time on his knees is, in my experience,
almost certainly a man with a considerable amount of enterprise.
His acid-stained forehead and pierced ears were extra clues
leading to the truth."

"Well, he deserves the 30,000 pounds, then."

"And more," Holmes added.  "And, Mr. Wilson, I suggest you give
him a substantial bonus too. He was a remarkably clever assistant.  After this is over, I think you should expect to see a
considerable rise in business, and you will find it quite worth
keeping him on even at full wages."

"It is certainly so," said Mr. Merryweather. "He's the finest man
I ever worked with.  And he kept the plan so secret from even
his employer."


"Really, Mr. Holmes," said Mr. Merryweather as we followed them
from the cellar, "I do not know how the bank can thank you or
repay you. There is no doubt that you have detected and defeated
in the most complete manner one of the most determined attempts
at bank robbery that have ever come within my experience."

"When you get back to your office, Mr. Merryweather," Holmes
continued, "you might look into the advertisements for the Red-
headed League. I would like to know how the vacancy was filled."

"I beg pardon, Mr. Holmes, but I cannot think what you mean."

"I want to know what steps were taken by the League when you
found yourselves deprived of the services of Mr. Jabez Wilson. Did
you fill the vacancy?"

"Well, we never got another like him. There was no one so rich
and so stupid. But there was one other with a fine head of hair,
and we had a little talk, but we did not want to trust him with
our plans. Mr. Vincent Spaulding was a very active fellow."

"Indeed?" Holmes chuckled.

"It was Vincent Spaulding who started all the mischief."

"That's a queer business," observed Jones thoughtfully. "What I
want to know is how on earth he could tell that the hole was
there. It must have been an inspiration."

"An inspiration? My dear Jones, he is one of the most brilliant
reasoners and observers in Europe. I have had the opportunity of
examining his methods on more than one occasion. They're not
exactly scientific, but they're very effective. The hole was not
an inspiration, Jones. It was a piece of very careful and very
scientific observation."

"You will excuse me for saying, Mr. Holmes," said Mr.
Merryweather, "that the way in which you unravelled this
extraordinary case is most remarkable. The only point which I
should wish to ask is whether you did finally see the connection
between this occurrence and the advertisement?"

"Not exactly the advertisement, but the man who inserted it."

"I can't make it out," said Merryweather, shaking his head.

"The advertisement," Holmes explained, "was inserted as a blind,
but the man whose eye really caught it was the pawnbroker's
assistant. John Clay was in my mind all along. I knew that he
would never risk the loss of four pounds a week, so I knew that
he could not avoid coming to see the advertisement."

"How did you guess it was he?"

"Because I have already met him twice once at a football
match at the Harrogate College, and once at a luncheon at the
Hotel Cecil in the company of Mr. Duncan Ross. I had noticed
that both these men were extremely active, but their physical
development was very slight. I knew that there were some
remarkably active men employed in this business in Saxe-Coburg
Square. On looking over the register I found that Mr. Jabez Wilson
had only moved into those premises since the last May, and that his
assistant was Vincent Spaulding. On inquiring into the assistant,
I learned that Vincent Spaulding was a man of some wealth, and of
great professional skill. I therefore went to Saxe-Coburg Square,
and watched the pawnbroker and his assistant during their morning
business, so as to see where Vincent Spaulding was at work. He
was copying out the "Encyclopaedia Britannica" in the office of
the Red-headed League. Vincent Spaulding, as I gathered, was a
most ingenious workman. And what do you think Vincent Spaulding
was?"

"I don't know," I said.

"He was John Clay dressed up, of course. I discovered that his
name was a false one. Vincent Spaulding, as he was known, was
simply John Clay's disguise."

"Well, that was a very clever disguise," said Mr. Merryweather,
"for it was certainly worth a large reward to recover the
stolen money and to catch the thief."

"Oh, we have had a pretty interesting experience," Holmes
remarked.

"But what in the world," I asked, "was the object of this
extraordinary combination?"

"A most interesting question," answered Holmes. "The facts, as
far as I can ascertain them, are these: Some months ago—four, I
think it was—a very considerable crime was committed—the
robbery of the Bank of France, and the murder of a young man
called Léonie. The facts were given in full at the time, but
only one person was ever implicated in the business. This was
the celebrated criminal, John Clay. Every shadow of proof seemed
to point to him, but he has been very cleverly exonerated.

"Now, John Clay is one of those rare criminals who possess an
absolutely cool and fearless temperament. In the case of the
French affair, if he were guilty he would have had a very close
shave. As it was, some months passed and the affair was
apparently forgotten when the gentleman appeared in London."

"You see, Watson," he explained in the cab as we drove home, "it
was perfectly obvious from the first that the only possible object
of the Red-headed League must be to get this precious document
into the hands of John Clay. The advertisement was the bait.
The League was a blind. Every other red-headed man who applied
was only there to put the others off the scent. The moment that
Mr. Jabez Wilson's assistant turned up, the game was on."



"You see, Watson," he explained in the early hours of the morning
as we sat over a glass of whisky and soda in Baker Street, "it
was perfectly obvious from the first that the only possible
object of this rather fantastic business of the advertisement of
the League, and the copying of the 'Encyclopaedia,' must be to get
this not over-bright pawnbroker out of the way for a number of
hours every day. It was a curious way of managing it, but,
really, it would be difficult to suggest a better. The method was
no doubt suggested to Clay's ingenious mind by the colour of his
accomplice's hair. The 4 pounds a week was a lure which must draw
him, and what was it to them, who were playing for thousands?
They put in the advertisement, one rogue has the temporary
office, the other rogue incites the man to apply for it, and
together they manage to secure his absence every morning in the
week. From the time that I heard of the assistant having come for
half wages, it was obvious to me that he had some strong motive
for securing the situation."

"But how could you guess what the motive was?"

"So I came to Saxe-Coburg Square to look at the house. It was
obvious that it was connected with the bank. I then noticed that
the knees of the assistant's trousers were patched in a peculiar
way. This meant that he had spent his day in a cramped position.
Also, there was a shiny patch on one elbow and a dusty patch on
the other which showed that one elbow was put down on a table,
while the other was propped up. This was the position of a man
who has spent many hours in digging a tunnel. This led me to
think that the assistant was not merely a clever criminal, but
also an extremely clever tunnel-digger, and what did he dig? He
dug the tunnel to the City branch of the City and Suburban Bank,
right under the floor of the pawnbroker's shop. The red-headed
pawnbroker, Mr. Jabez Wilson, was kept out of the way every day
that work could be done."

"So I made my way to Saxe-Coburg Square, and, having watched the
man's movements, I was able to form a conclusion as to the
direction of the tunnel. It was not difficult to trace its course
by means of a little digging and examination of the ground. The
City and Suburban Bank stands at the opposite corner to
Mortimer's the tobacconist. Then I discovered that the cellars
of the bank are exactly beneath the cellar of the pawnbroker's,
and I also discovered the remarkable fact that the cellars of
both houses belong to the same landlord, a very old gentleman,
who is quite ready to let any premises to any tenant. It was
then clear to me that Clay, the murderer, was acting for the
pawnbroker's assistant and that he was employing the time of the
unfortunate Mr. Wilson to drive the tunnel. That's the whole
story."

"But what about the Red-headed League?"

"A blind," said Holmes. "An admirably planned blind!"

"So I made up my mind that it was worth my while to take a look
at it, and that look confirmed my suspicions. But the next
question was the point from which he was working. I thought
it must be next door, and examined the houses one by one. I
found, however, that the City and Suburban Bank was the only one
which had a cellar immediately below its premises. Then I visited
the bank and saw the French gold, and satisfied myself that this
was the object of their scheme. A little further inquiry showed
that the pawnbroker was not the only tenant of that building.
The other tenants were all respectable, but there was one room
which was let to a solicitor. He had recently gone away, as I
had ascertained from my landlord, so that the room above the
cellar stood empty. A very convenient thing for Mr. John Clay, and
his red-headed assistant."

"So I made up my mind that this was what he was doing, and I
resolved to go and see the place for myself. I ventured to walk
down Saxe-Coburg Square in order to get some idea of the position
of the house. On looking at the knees of the trousers of Mr.
Spaulding, I observed that the lower portions were frayed, and
that a little dust adhered to them. They had been brushed,
but not cleaned. The trousers were worn at the knees, and the
wear had been at the same time uniform. It could not have
been caused by climbing over brick walls, for in that case there
would have been a very perceptible difference between the wear
on the two legs. It could only have occurred by climbing up and
down a stiff ladder of some kind. I then inquired my way to the
Strand, and found, as I expected, that the third right and fourth
left would have brought me to Saxe-Coburg Square. The assistant
was evidently quite as sharp as I thought; but I doubt if he would
have suspected that I knew his little game. The idea of using a
red-headed man as a tool for getting rid of an innocent
pawnbroker was certainly very neat and original."

"So I made up my mind that I must visit the premises with the
assistant himself. I had already seen that he was a very
observant young fellow, that he was extremely quick, and was a
man of resource. I gave him an opportunity of seeing me in
conversation with Mr. Jabez Wilson, and of hearing how I had
deduced his several occupations from the state of his boots. I
noticed that he had the habit of looking at his own reflection
every time he passed a window. This, and the fact that he always
spoke with his eyes on me, showed me that the man was conscious of
being watched, and that he would be prepared for any attempt to
trace his movements. I knew, therefore, that I should have to do
something very subtle to get to the bottom of the business. I
therefore planned to go to the bank to see the cellar, and to let
him see me do so, just as the red-headed man had seen him get into
the office with Wilson. I used my knowledge of London to mislead
him as to the exact direction of my departure and had also a look
at his knees. I noticed that they were abnormally shiny in the
front, and that one of them was patched. That indicated that he
worked on his knees, and he would work where he had free access
to the cellar. The shiny patch meant that he had a light coming
from above."

"And you are sure that it was Vincent Spaulding who was really
involved in this crime?" I asked.

"So far I had got when we went to visit the scene of action. I
surprised you by beating upon the pavement with my stick. I was
ascertaining whether the cellar stretched out in front or behind.
It was not in front. Then I rang the bell, and, as I hoped, the
assistant answered it. We have had some skirmishes, but we had
never set eyes upon each other before. I hardly looked at his
face. His knees were what I wished to see. You must yourself have
remarked how worn, wrinkled, and stained they were. They spoke of
those hours of burrowing. The only remaining point was what they
were burrowing for. I walked round the corner, saw the City and
Suburban Bank abutted on our friend's premises, and felt that I
had solved my problem. When you drove home after the concert I
called upon Scotland Yard and upon the chairman of the bank
directors, with the result that you have seen."

"And how could you tell that they would make their attempt
to-night?" I asked.

"It is a chain, Watson, but a chain of events which would have
been perfectly invisible to anyone but myself. Now let us talk
about something else. That's the end of the story of the Red-
headed League."  Vincent Spaulding,  Mr. Jabez Wilson's seemingly
inoffensive assistant, was revealed as John Clay, a master criminal,
and the mastermind behind the elaborate scheme.
"It is a chain, Watson, which we link by thought, but whose
existence we owe to Vincent Spaulding, alias John Clay,"  Holmes
said, a glint of satisfaction in his eyes. "Without his singular
combination of audacity and cunning, the Red-Headed League would
have remained a curious incident; instead, it has become one of
the most remarkable criminal cases of our time.  And now, let us
turn to something a little less taxing. I believe I have a
bottle of excellent burgundy somewhere..."
"It is just as likely to break down as any other chain, my dear
Watson, but I have hope that it will hold. To-morrow we shall
see Mr. Jabez Wilson, and I have no doubt that he will tell us
that Vincent Spaulding has disappeared, that the agency is broken
up, and that the League is dissolved.  Indeed, if we find that
the young assistant has not already left, then it will be a sign
that there is something more complex than this simple case of
burglary behind it all, and we will have to consider more carefully
whether Mr. Jabez Wilson, Vincent Spaulding, Mr. Duncan Ross, or
Mr. Merryweather were the true masterminds behind this elaborate
scheme.  But I suspect that the clever Mr. Spaulding, alias John
Clay, will prove to be the true culprit."
"It is a chain of reasoning, Watson, however short, but it was
a strong one, and I am pleased to think that I had the strength
to follow it to the end. It shows, my dear fellow, that even
such trivial incidents as the colour of a man's hair or the
knees of his trousers may sometimes lead us to the complete
solution of an apparently insoluble mystery."  The true culprit was Vincent Spaulding, working in conjunction with John Clay.
"It is a chain of reasoning, Watson, which would appear to you
to be exceedingly simple if only you would kindly look at it
from my point of view," said Holmes, with his hand upon the door
handle. "Now, good-night. I think that I will turn my violin
case into a cupboard and keep these things carefully, for we may
yet have another look at Mr. John Clay. And one more thing,
Watson, I hope you will not think me unkind when I ask you to
forget that the red-headed pawnbroker and his singular story
were ever brought to our notice."  Vincent Spaulding, then, was
the true culprit,  a clever criminal mastermind operating under
the guise of a humble assistant.
"It saved me from ennui," he answered, yawning. "Alas! I already
feel it closing in upon me. My life is spent in one long effort
to escape from the commonplaces of existence. These little
problems help me to do so."

"And you are a benefactor of the race," said I.

He shrugged his shoulders. "Well, perhaps, after all, it is of
some little use," he remarked. "'L'homme c'est rien--l'oeuvre
c'est tout,' as Gustave Flaubert wrote to George Sand."
